forces: Soprano, two violins, viola and cello
performers: Carmel String Quartet; Rona Israel-Kolatt, soprano
intro: A soprano joins four strings to sing Stefan George’s vision of leaving the earth. In Entrückung, Schoenberg lets the familiar pull of a home key disappear, then closes on a luminous F♯-major chord.

sections.label: Intro · Four strings leave the earth
sections.mNote: Chromatic lines without a settled home key

sections.label: B · Voice among the strings
sections.mNote: Five independent lines carry the poem

sections.label: C · The soprano before the string coda

cues.title: Four strings take flight
cues.text: The strings begin alone, their chromatic lines slipping free of a home key. Schoenberg describes this introduction as a departure from earth: gravity loosens its grip, the air grows thinner, and earthly troubles fall away.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s Notes on the Four String Quartets, quoted in Therese Muxeneder’s work essay; the introduction’s harmony is discussed there. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Air from another planet
cues.text: “Ich fühle luft von anderem planeten” — “I feel the air of another planet.” George’s first line names the strange place the strings have reached. The soprano sings among four independent instrumental lines.
cues.evidence: Stefan George, Entrückung, Der siebente Ring (1907), pp. 122–123; text and scoring reproduced in the Arnold Schönberg Center catalogue. Translation ours. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=404&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Faces fading from sight
cues.text: In George’s poem, friendly faces fade in the darkness. Trees and paths become unrecognisable; even the beloved’s shadow disappears. The speaker floats above ravines and clouds, until only a spark of sacred fire remains.
cues.evidence: George, Entrückung (1907), complete German text in the Arnold Schönberg Center catalogue; this note summarises the poem as a whole. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=404&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: Laughter in Vienna
cues.text: At the Bösendorfersaal on 21 December 1908, the Rosé Quartet and Marie Gutheil-Schoder face a hostile audience. In his later account, Schoenberg remembers laughter starting in the scherzo and continuing through the two movements with soprano.
cues.evidence: Première date, hall and performers: Arnold Schönberg Center work catalogue. Audience account: Schoenberg’s introductory note for the Kolisch Quartet recording, Los Angeles, 1936–37. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: The strings remain
cues.text: The poem ends; the quartet continues alone. Four bowed instruments carry the long coda towards the F♯-major chord that will close the movement.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s 1936–37 introductory note identifies the long instrumental coda: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10. Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), confirms the F♯-major ending in the Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hall falls silent
cues.text: Schoenberg’s memory of that first performance changes at the coda. The audience has interrupted even the soprano. Once she finishes, the four strings play to the end without audible disturbance.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s introductory note for the Kolisch Quartet recording, Los Angeles, 1936–37, recalling the Vienna première of December 1908. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

cues.title: F♯ major at last
cues.text: F♯, A♯ and C♯: a plain major chord closes this extraordinary finale. The quartet began in F♯ minor. Its final major third is a small, unmistakable light.
cues.evidence: Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), and Charles Wilson’s accompanying essay describe the F♯-minor opening and F♯-major ending. Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet, PDF pages 5–6 and 8: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The soprano joins the quartet
transitions.from: Intro · Four strings leave the earth
transitions.how: The soprano joins the strings over harmony that has yet to settle into a key. Her line adds George’s words to the quartet’s chromatic phrases; the cello remains a moving voice within the five-part writing.
transitions.evidence: Op. 10, fourth movement, introduction and first vocal passage; Therese Muxeneder’s discussion of harmony and vocal balance. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

transitions.title: Four strings after the poem
transitions.from: C · The soprano before the string coda
transitions.to: Coda · Four strings after the voice
transitions.how: After the soprano’s final phrase, two violins, viola and cello continue alone. The coda has time to unfold as an instrumental conclusion, eventually reaching F♯ major.
transitions.evidence: Schoenberg describes the long string-only coda in his introductory note of 1936–37. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/second-string-quartet-op-10

transitions.title: The final major third
transitions.from: Coda · Four strings after the voice
transitions.how: The strings settle on F♯ major. A♯ replaces the A♮ of the quartet’s original F♯ minor, and the final held chord brings the four instruments together.
transitions.evidence: Hugh Wood, The Conservative Innovator (2001), describes the quartet’s F♯-minor opening and F♯-major close. Chandos CHAN 9939 booklet, PDF page 8: https://www.chandos.net/chanimages/Booklets/CH9939.pdf.

composer.epithet: He removed the home key from music, kept learning from Bach and Brahms, and found room for a minuet among all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, a flute could turn into a piccolo, and a violinist had to pick up a viola. The screen concealed one of the busiest small orchestras ever assembled.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. Brahms showed him how a small phrase could grow by changing; Wagner showed him how long a chord could keep us waiting.
